chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Abu Ayoub, from Abu Hamza al-Thumali, who said:

A man said to Ali ibn al-Husayn (peace be upon him): 'Have you left Jihad and its hardship, and adhered to Hajj and its ease?' He said: 'And he (peace be upon him) was reclining, so he sat up and said: 'Woe to you! Has it not reached you what the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said during the Farewell Pilgrimage? Indeed, when he stood at Arafat and the sun inclined to set, the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'O Bilal! Say to the people, so let them be silent.' So when they were silent, the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'Your Lord has extended favor upon you in this day, so He forgave your good-doers, and your good-doers interceded for your evil-doers. Therefore depart, forgiven for you.'
He said: 'And others than al-Thumali added that he said: 'Except for the people of liabilities (debts/obligations), for Allah is Just. He takes for the weak from the strong.'

So when it was the night of Jam' (Arafat), he did not cease to converse with his Lord and ask Him for the people of liabilities. So when he stood at Jam', he said to Bilal: 'Say to the people, so let them be silent!' So when they were silent, he said: 'Your Lord has extended favor upon you in this day, so He forgave your good-doers, and your good-doers interceded for your evil-doers. Therefore depart, forgiven for you, and He guaranteed for the people of liabilities from His presence the satisfaction (of their creditors).'

key_terms.أَهْلَ التَّبِعَاتِ: People of liabilities (those with debts/obligations to others)

ai.seo_question: What is the significance of 'liabilities' (tabi'at) in the Prophet's Farewell Sermon at Arafat?
ai.summary: Imam Ali ibn al-Husayn (Zayn al-Abidin) refutes the notion that Hajj is inferior to Jihad by highlighting the unique spiritual efficacy of the Day of Arafat, where divine mercy is amplified through intercession. He specifically addresses the 'Ahl al-Taba'at' (those with financial or social obligations to others), whose sins are often hindered by unpaid debts, by narrating that God guarantees their satisfaction (Rida) from the Divine treasury. This tradition underscores the Shia emphasis on social justice and the purification of the soul through settling rights (Huquq al-Ibad) as a prerequisite for complete spiritual acceptance.
